stories.registration-problem: {{cast.user}} asks {{cast.assistant}} to rebook a flight. {{cast.assistant}} has never talked to the {{cast.resource}} before, and {{cast.company}} would rather not hand-register every assistant a customer brings along.
stories.idea: {{cast.assistant}} publishes one JSON file at {{cast.clientUrl}}. That address is its id. The {{cast.resource}} reads the file instead of keeping a record made in advance.
stories.document: The file at {{cast.clientUrl}} names {{cast.client}}, lists the one callback it will accept, and carries no secret, because anyone can read it.
stories.strict: {{cast.company}}'s sign-in server does not trust the address just because {{cast.assistant}} typed it. It fetches over https only, refuses private addresses, caps the size, and checks the file names itself.
stories.direction1: Here the lab plays {{cast.assistant}}'s side and a real PingFederate plays {{cast.company}}'s sign-in server. Whether PingFederate accepts a URL as a client id is exactly what the owner checks, and it is not claimed here.
stories.probe: The probe sends {{cast.client}}'s address to PingFederate. A sign-in page means it fetched and accepted the file; an HTTP 400 means no policy there matches that address.
stories.direction2: Now the lab plays {{cast.company}}'s sign-in server. It receives {{cast.client}}'s address from {{cast.user}}'s trip, fetches the file and shows {{cast.user}} a consent screen built from it.
stories.refusals: A look-alike assistant claims to be {{cast.client}} but its file names a different id, or hides a secret in the open. The server stops it at the named check, and {{cast.user}} never sees a consent screen.
stories.close: {{cast.company}} saves the registration step and keeps the trust where it belongs: in the file and in how strictly the server reads it. Reset clears the lab for the next audience.
